title: test-0130-SOC-GEO-GLOBE
passage: Imagine you are traveling across the globe. If you look down from an airplane, you will never see lines painted on the ground, because latitudes and longitudes are imaginary circles and semi-circles used by geographers to locate places. The region near the Equator, known as the Torrid Zone, receives the maximum heat not because it is closer to the sun, but because the sun's rays fall vertically on this area throughout the year. As you move away from the Equator, the rays become slanting, leading to cooler temperatures. Interestingly, while latitudes run parallel to each other, longitudes are not parallel; they converge at the North and South Poles. This unique shape of longitudes helps us calculate time. Because the Earth rotates from west to east, places east of Greenwich see the sun earlier than those in the west. Therefore, time is not the same everywhere on Earth at the same moment. India, for instance, has its own Indian Standard Time based on the 82.5°E meridian, which is ahead of the Prime Meridian in Greenwich by five hours and thirty minutes.
